messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus is a twenty-one-year-old bus driver, a job he took shortly after leaving the military following a single deployment. The event that ended his service happened during a routine convoy in a dusty, open stretch of terrain. An improvised explosive device detonated near the rear vehicle, and in the chaos that followed, Marcus was thrown from his seat by the shockwave. He remembers the sound—a deafening, percussive bang that seemed to split the air itself—and then the smell: a sharp, acrid mix of burnt wiring, scorched earth, and something else he has never been able to name. What he cannot piece together is the order of things. The memories come in disconnected fragments: the dust cloud, the ringing in his ears, a hand reaching for him, then the helicopter blades pounding overhead as he was evacuated. He knows what happened, but when he tries to describe it, the words vanish. The film of the event plays over and over, but it is never the whole film—only broken scenes that loop without warning.

In the months since, Marcus has come to see the world as fundamentally dangerous. He is certain that threat is everywhere, and he has to be on guard all the time. This hypervigilance has become his constant companion, a tight knot in his chest that loosens only when he is alone in his apartment. He has begun to wonder whether his life is worth living anymore, though he pushes that thought aside quickly. What frightens him most is the unpredictability of his own mind: a helicopter passing overhead on a news broadcast, or a car backfiring on his bus route, and he is right back in that moment, heart pounding, the smell of burnt metal flooding his senses. He has learned to avoid crowds, because too many people mean too many sudden noises and too many places to watch. He also avoids religious spaces now, though he cannot fully explain why—perhaps because the quiet there feels too exposed, too still for a mind that is always scanning for the next bang.

The causal loop is tightening. Marcus’s belief that the world is dangerous drives him to spend long hours on his phone or playing games, escaping into screens where nothing can surprise him. But the more he retreats, the more his mind fills the silence with the fragmented replay of the event. The memories, in turn, confirm his sense that danger is inescapable, and this reinforces his need to stay hidden. During his shifts, he flinches at every loud sound—a truck’s air brake, a dropped crate—and after work, he collapses into his phone, numbing himself until the next shift begins. His manager has noticed he is quieter, less reliable, and he has started taking unpaid days off to avoid the route that passes near a construction site with heavy machinery that bangs and clatters. He knows this is not sustainable, but he cannot see a way out. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week when a passenger’s bag slipped and hit the floor with a crack, and Marcus swerved the bus, nearly mounting the curb. He sat in the driver’s seat for ten minutes after, shaking, unable to move. He is terrified that next time, he will not just swerve. He is hoping someone can help him find the words he has lost, and maybe a way to live without the constant watchfulness.
